In many countries where undernutrition is widespread, food production is not the limiting factor, with the exception of famine
cases. The most important factors are, ﬁrstly, insufﬁcient knowledge about the beneﬁts of exclusive breastfeeding, complementary
feeding practices and the function of micronutrients, and secondly, the lack of time women have to adequately care for their babies
or for themselves during pregnancy. The most pernicious effects of undernutrition occur during pregnancy and the ﬁrst 2 years of
life, and the consequences of such early damage to health, brain development, intelligence, and to possibilities of beneﬁting from
education and productivity are largely irreversible. There is evidence suggesting that obesity and NCDs such as cardiovascular
disease and diabetes may also have their origins in early childhood. Moreover, the increase in overweight in conjunction with per-
sisting undernutrition in young children has led to the aforementioned double burden of malnutrition in many countries, and
studies have shown that both undernutrition and overweight have similar causes. As such, some have criticized the classiﬁcation
of malnutrition into under and overnutrition as being simplistic due to the interrelated nature between the two.
Determinants
Biological and dietary factors
Maternal undernutrition can result in intrauterine undernutrition and low birth weight, among others. Insufﬁcient food intake to
allow for compensatory growth that could offset this situation brings about the onset of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in early
life stages.
